newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egyptian heavy metal fans tread in deep water.
newsitem.headline: Egyptian heavy metal fans tread in deep water.

text.p: A bunch of Egyptian rich kids with attitude and a taste for heavy metal has found out the hard way that Egyptian society may not be ready for black leather, skull tattoos or flirtation with Satanic ritual.

A fad which elsewhere would compete with a host of other youth subcultures -- punks, skinheads, Hell's Angels or New Agers -- is the talk of the town as the establishment gets to grips with what it sees as a cultural invasion.

The Mufti, leading exponent of Islamic law, has spoken darkly of apostasy and punishment. Parliament, in a debate on Satanism on Sunday, passed a motion condemning what it called "deviation from the traditions of Egyptian society".

Some of the heavy metal fans, especially those who organised rock concerts at public places in Cairo over the last three years, languish in custody under interrogation by incredulous State Security officers who think the Beatles are risque.
They could face charges of contempt for religion, for which the maximum penalty under Egyptian law is three years in prison.

Government newspapers, in daily doses of shock and horror, relate how the "Satanists" sacrificed cats, took part in group sex, called up the devil on ouija boards and performed Satanic rituals at Cairo cemeteries.
Materials supposed to incriminate them include Megadeath, Metallica and Black Sabbath albums and posters and T-shirts with Gothic symbols like skulls and inverted crosses.
The fans obtained these from mysterious foreigners bent on spreading the devil cult and who "smuggled" them in.
Judging by the howls of outrage from the men in grey suits, Egyptian society is in serious danger of collapse as the Satanists erode the moral fibre of a devout and pious nation.

"Is it possible that such deviance should exist in Egypt -- Egypt the country of faith and monotheism since the dawn of history?" asked Mustafa Kamal Hilmi, the speaker of the Shoura (consultative) chamber of parliament.
"We applaud the vigilance of the security agencies that uncovered this misguided cult," he added.
"We must deal decisively with this errant group, which has gone beyond the pale of society," said member Tharwat Abaza.
The Mufti, Nasr Farid Wassil, said the "Satanists" were apostates from Islam but the right approach, in view of their youth, was to ask them to repent.

"If they renounce their beliefs, they can be pardoned. But if they persist in their error, we should carry out the penalty prescribed by Islamic law," added the Mufti, quoted in the newpaper al-Akhbar. The penalty for apostasy is death.

But details from the interrogations, leaked to the weekly magazine Rose el-Youssef, suggest that many of those under interrogation were in it just for the sex, the drugs and the rock and roll or, at the most, to shock their elders.
"One of the accused said he was imitating foreigners. Most of the accused justified joining the group by saying they liked the music," the magazine said.
"I don't have anything to do with Satanism," said one of them. "I joined because their parties were exciting. I used to go to feel up the girls when they were dancing," he added.
"We use the inverted cross, not to worship it, but because it's cool. We were just fooling around," said one informant.

But others did show signs they took the Satan cult seriously, in rebellion against the pervasive religious orthodoxy of Egyptian society. "Satan permits quick pleasure, he permits things forbidden by other religions," a heavy metal fan named as Tareq Hassan told the prosecutors.
"The other reason (for joining) is to be unconventional, to be individual and look different," he added.

Rose el-Youssef, in an anguished analysis of the phenomenon, said: "It indicates there are thousands of youngsters looking for fulfilment, to prove their identity, to declare they are rebels...even if that means addiction to Satanic rock."
"It is a generation that feels alienated, that has formed a cultural ghetto and joined a counter-culture," it added.
